Splendour] ‘Dream, poetic imagining’ (GM); a Dantean word, especially in the Paradiso (e.g. ix
13–15, xxi 32, xxiii 82–3). Cp. Taaffe ‘Annotations’: ‘This term Splendour for any immaterial sub-
stance is borrowed from Dante’ (Fogle 39).
 Cp. Pope, An Essay on Criticism i 150–7:
Thus Pegasus, a nearer way to take,
May boldly deviate from the common track.
 Great wits sometimes may gloriously offend,
And rise to faults true critics dare not mend;
From vulgar bounds with brave disorder part,
And snatch a grace beyond the reach of art,
Which without passing through the judgment, gains
The heart, and all its end at once attains.
 S.’s deployment of the allusion in ll. 101–4 turns Pope’s famous lines to Keats’s advantage, and implic-
itly rebukes the anonymous critic who had attacked Keats for his idiosyncratic stylistic mannerisms.
